paper_title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Human brain encoding models predict neural responses to stimuli, providing computational insights into how the brain processes information. State-of-the-art (SoTA) encoding models mostly follow goal-driven paradigm (Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016): large model pretrained on behavioral tasks is used as frozen feature extractor, and only readout is learned from neural data (Adeli et al., 2025; Hwang et al., 2025; Gokce et al., 2026a; dAscoli et al., 2026). This approach leverages strong pretrained priors, but misses the opportunity to exploit the backbones expressiveness to specialize for brain encoding. Adapting large pretrained backbones with neural data promises to scale models to the complexity required to capture human brain computation, and to best combine neural information and behavioral task training. In practice, however, such adaptation is difficult, because neural data are costly and scarce relative to the size of contemporary models. Methods that do let neural data shape the representation have had mixed success. 1 Figure 1 From frozen backbones to PEFT, and three directions to scale PEFT for brain encoding. (a) The dominant paradigm: frozen pretrained backbone with readouts trained for brain encoding. The backbone prior is strong, but it is not specialized for brain encoding. (b) We advocate using PEFT to adapt strong pretrained backbones, retaining the powerful prior while allowing flexible neural adaptation. This suggests three complementary scaling directions: Scale up to stronger priors leveraging more capable backbones; Scale down the size of trainable adapters for brain encoding with limited data; and Scale out the number of adapters with different specializations. Training smaller models from scratch (St-Yves et al., 2023; Khosla and Wehbe, 2026) has not reached SoTA performance on whole-brain human benchmarks, and full fine-tuning of pretrained backbone has been reported to underperform freezing it (Yang et al., 2023). Low-rank adaptation won Algonauts 2023 (Yang et al., 2023), but only with relatively small ViT, and it has not been tested on large multimodal models. We argue that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is powerful yet underexplored regime for building strong brain encoding models. It retains the strong prior and expressive capacity of large pretrained model and allows limited neural data to adapt its representations through small set of parameters (3). While the framework applies to any pretrained backbone, stimulus modality, or neural recording, we evaluate it in particularly demanding setting: the CNeuroMod/Algonauts 2025 Challenge (Gifford et al., 2025), which requires predicting whole-brain fMRI responses to long, naturalistic audiovisual movies and tests generalization to held-out out-of-distribution stimuli. We show below that PEFT is powerful at scale, setting new SoTA on this benchmark while remaining efficient. We first make large-scale adaptation for brain encoding computationally practical. Prior approaches typically rely on overlapping sliding windows for feature extraction, resulting in substantial redundant computation of shared stimulus context. By exploiting the backbones innate causal masking, we encode each training window in single forward pass and obtain representations for all timesteps simultaneously (Antonello et al., 2023). This reduces feature-extraction cost by approximately 350 relative to the sliding-window protocol used by the prior SoTA at little performance cost (Gokce et al., 2026a; 4). With adaptation made practical, we show that low-rank adapter (LoRA; Hu et al., 2021) consistently improves brain encoding on all nine multimodal backbones we test, spanning 4.7B104B parameters, the largest models ever adapted to brain encoding to our knowledge. On the same backbone Qwen3-Omni as the prior SoTA (Gokce et al., 2026a), our method BrainLoRA pairs LoRA with lightweight readout. With only about 5% as many trainable parameters, BrainLoRA sets new SoTA among published methods (5.1 and 5.2). Moreover, we show the adapted multimodal model remains interpretable. Prior work often identifies regions preferred modality by determining which unimodal encoder its readout relies on. With multimodal backbones, we instead use feature attribution to identify modality contribution, which recovers the canonical topography: 2 early visual cortex is driven by video, and auditory and lateral temporal cortex by audio. Comparison with the frozen backbone shows that adaptation reweights the contributions of the three modalities, particularly increasing the contribution of the audio inputs, and increases cross-modal mixing within the backbone (5.4). Finally, to scale the number of adapted models, we develop batched multi-LoRA kernel that trains many LoRAs jointly on one shared backbone, significantly reducing training time. This enables 200+ independently adapted models, whose ensemble ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard, surpassing unpublished entries as well. We additionally show that the ensemble performance is jointly governed by ensemble size, individual model quality, and model diversity (5.5). Together, our results suggest three complementary scaling directions for future brain encoding models under the PEFT paradigm: Scale up the pretrained prior by leveraging increasingly capable backbones; Scale down the adaptation with neural data by updating only small number of parameters; and Scale out by training large number of lightweight adapters to shared backbone with varying specializations (Fig. 1b; 3). Together, PEFT turns single powerful pretrained model into family of specialized encoding models without paying the cost of training each model from scratch. Our contributions are as follows: Efficiency. We make PEFT on large multimodal backbones computationally practical for brain encoding (4), reducing feature-extraction cost by 350 via single-pass extraction compared to prior SoTA (Gokce et al., 2026a) and accelerating multi-LoRA training significantly with batched training kernel. Effectiveness. LoRA consistently improves performance over frozen backbones on all nine multimodal backbones we test (5.1). LoRA with lightweight readout beats the previous published SoTA on both ID and OOD test sets using 5% as many trainable parameters (5.2). Interpretability. We show that large multimodal backbones for brain encoding remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders. Comparing with the frozen backbone reveals that adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and the degree of cross-modal mixing in the backbone (5.4). Scalability. We scale the backbone up to 104B multimodal models, the largest backbones adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge, and scale out to 200+ independently adapted models (5.5). The ensemble ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: We organize related works by where the neural signal enters the encoding model pipeline (see the extended related work in App. A). Frozen backbone, trained readout. Most brain encoding methods use pretrained task-optimized backbones as frozen feature extractors and train readouts to predict neural responses (Naselaris et al., 2011; Huth et al., 2016; Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016; Schrimpf et al., 2021). All top-ranked entries in the Algonauts 2025 challenge (Gifford et al., 2025) followed this paradigm (Gokce et al., 2026a; dAscoli et al., 2026; Carlström Schad et al., 2025). Compared to more classic voxel-wise ridge regression methods (Naselaris et al., 2011), recent top-performing models have been using more expressive and flexible readout (dAscoli et al., 2026; Adeli et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025), yet the training is still confined to only the readout module. Backbones fine-tuned by brain data. Much fewer studies have instead directly adapted pretrained models using neural data. Brain-tuning of language and speech models improves not only alignment but downstream semantic tasks (Schwartz et al., 2019; Moussa et al., 2025; Moussa and Toneva, 2025), and the vision analogue gains robustness and behavioral alignment (Li et al., 2019; Federer et al., 2020). PEFT is already used within this family: MEM uses LoRA on vision backbones and won Algonauts 2023 (Yang et al., 2023); BrainWavLM matches full fine-tune with LoRA adaptation (Vattikonda et al., 2025); Scholz et al. (2025) uses LoRA on 3B Llama model on Algonauts 2025 and ranked 10th. Our work follows this direction but extends it to substantially larger model scale: to our knowledge, prior models above 15B parameters have been used only as frozen feature extractors, whereas we directly adapt backbones up to 104B. Other ways to incorporate neural data. Other approaches incorporate neural signals through auxiliary alignment objectives (Dapello et al., 2023; Gokce et al., 2026b), yet shuffled-target controls sometimes re3 produce much of the reported benefit (Guo et al., 2025); through self-supervised pretraining on neural data alone (Ortega Caro et al., 2024; Lane et al., 2026), which captures intrinsic neural dynamics rather than stimulus-referred computation (Zahorodnii et al., 2025); through unified stimulusbrain models (Wu et al., 2026), or train the model on neural data from scratch (Lurz et al., 2021; Klindt et al., 2017; St-Yves et al., 2023; Khosla and Wehbe, 2026), none of which, however, are yet outperforming brain encoders built on large task-optimized feature backbones on public benchmarks (Schrimpf et al., 2018; Gifford et al., 2025).

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: Task and data. We evaluate on CNeuroMod/Algonauts 2025 (Boyle et al., 2023; Gifford et al., 2025) challenge, which contains whole-brain fMRI recordings, parcellated into 1,000 regions (Schaefer et al., 2018), from subjects viewing seven seasons of Friends, with synchronized video, audio, and transcript. We train on four subjects, validate on Season 6, and evaluate on held-out Season 7 (ID) and movies (OOD). Our main experiments use Qwen3-Omni (Xu et al., 2025), the same as the best published method (Gokce et al., 2026a), for controlled comparison. We also conduct experiments on diverse set of nine backbones (Tab. 10, 12). Single-pass extraction. The prior SoTA (Gokce et al., 2026a) predicts each fMRI timestep from an overlapping sliding window, with 2,800 forward passes per clip (Fig. 2a). However, since the backbone is already causally masked, much of the repeated computation of sliding window is unnecessary. We therefore encode each 149 window (100 TRs) with single forward pass and extract representations for all timesteps simultaneously (Fig. 2b), an approach more common in language encoding models (Antonello et al., 2023). This single-pass design reduces feature-extraction cost by 350 relative to the sliding-window protocol of Gokce et al. (2026a) (from about 700 to 2 GPU-hours on A800), making fine-tuning through the backbone computationally affordable. Under frozen readout, single-pass features incur only small performance drop, which we attribute mainly to missing stimulus context at the start of each window (Tab. 3). We thus incorporate 60s context lead that largely recovers it  (Fig. 6)  . With LoRA fine-tuning, our configuration surpasses the original sliding-window baseline (App. B). 4 The modality encoders preceding the decoder are locally bidirectional, over 8s of audio blocks and 1s of visual patches. To assess the effect of this limited non-causality, we re-encode strict prefixes of each input and compare representations at shared timesteps (App. F). We observe small differences, which are mainly attributable to length-dependent bf16 MoE numerics, instead of leakage of future stimuli (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). PEFT for Brain Encoding. For our main method on Qwen3-Omni, we insert rank-16 LoRA into the attention modules through layer 32 and truncate the decoder at this layer, introducing 8.91M trainable parameters. The adapters and readout are jointly optimized for one epoch. For hyperparameter tuning, see App. E. We also show that other PEFT methods like IA3 (Liu et al., 2022) and adapter layers (Houlsby et al., 2019) show similar effects (App. H). Readout. We use linear or cross-attention (Adeli et al., 2025) readouts. Backbone features are pooled into one vector per modality at each 2 Hz timestep and aggregated into eight log-spaced temporal-lag blocks aligned with the fMRI sampling rate. final linear projection maps to 1,000 brain parcels, with 52.3M trainable parameters. We pool the original 19.3k tokens to 894 vectors per input window. As an alternative, we replace the fixed temporal-lag aggregation with per-TR cross-attention over an expanded set of 3.2k tokens, adding only 0.2M parameters. Ablations in 5.3 attribute the improvement of cross-attention over linear readout primarily to the access to the richer token set. Figure 2 One causally masked pass replaces sliding window. The baseline re-encodes an overlapping window per fMRI timestep; single pass over the window gives features at every timestep. Closed-form re-fit. After joint optimization with SGD, we re-fit the linear readout in closed form. Forward passes accumulate subject-specific Gram matrices, after which is solved using parcel-wise ridge regression following Nunez-Elizalde et al. (2019). As shown in 5.3, the improvement primarily arises from the closed-form re-estimation rather than the parcel-specific regularization.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: We use the mean Pearson correlation across the four subjects as the primary fMRI prediction metric. The seed-to-seed variability is small: methods whose mean correlations differ by less than 0.00077 cannot be reliably separated (LoRA+linear with 15 seeds; App. D). We therefore support each method comparison using seed variations whenever multiple runs are available, or for two single models, paired bootstrap over parcels, which tests whether the performance difference holds across the cortex.

sections.title: 5.2 A small adapter beats a large readout
sections.content: As shown in Tab. 1, the previous single-model SoTA, MIRAGE (Gokce et al., 2026a), uses frozen backbone plus 1.1B-parameter transformer-based readout. In contrast, our LoRA+linear model trains only 61.2M parameters (5% of MIRAGE) and already outperforms it on both ID and OOD test sets  (Fig. 7)  . Replacing the linear readout with cross-attention, our best single model method, BrainLoRA, further improves performance to 0.327 on ID and 0.228 on OOD, exceeding the published 15-model MIRAGE ensemble on ID and matching it on OOD, setting new SoTA on the Algonauts challenge. Ensembling population of 200+ models further reaches 0.343 on ID and 0.248 on OOD, achieving the highest score on the public leaderboard at the time of writing (5.5). Selecting subset of 15 models still maintains strong performance. Full fine-tuning of all 20.25B parameters below the feature extraction layer reaches 0.323 (linear) and 0.330 (cross-attention) on validation, on par with or slightly below the corresponding LoRA configurations, with 330 more trainable parameters. The held-out test sets show the same patterns, with larger decrease on OOD (Tab. 1). Full fine-tuning thus does not outperform LoRA at this data scale, consistent with prior works (Yang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Moussa and Toneva, 2025; Vattikonda et al., 2025). The adaptation transfers to unseen subjects and new dataset. The learned adaptation generalizes beyond both the subjects and the dataset used for training, with gains essentially matching those observed in-distribution. When trained on three subjects and evaluated on held-out fourth subject with the LoRAs frozen and only the readout re-fitted, it retains 97% of the improvement observed for subjects included in LoRA training (App. M). The same adapter and readout also transfer zero-shot to the Naturalistic Neuroimaging Database (NNDb; Aliko et al., 2020), collected at different site with different scanner and repetition time, and with subjects viewing films. The adapter is applied without any further training on NNDb, including the readout. Even so, it yields gain of +11.1 percentage points of the noise ceiling, on par with the +10.7-point fine-tuning gain on our validation set (App. N). With only minutes of new subjects data, solving its readout as correction to the population readout improves the transfer performance 6 (App. O). The adapter thus captures stimulus representations that generalize to other subjects or datasets.

sections.title:
5.4 Interpreting the multimodal backbone
Encoding models can be used to ask which stimulus information is processed, and therefore drives the
prediction of neural activity, in a given brain region. Prior work often answers this by construction, using
separate unimodal backbones so that a region’s preferred modality or semantic selectivity can be read off
directly from the readout by the weights or the attention patterns (Adeli et al., 2025; d’Ascoli et al., 2026). A
single multimodal backbone, however, lacks this explicit separation, with information from different modalities
merging early in the backbone. We show that feature attribution methods can estimate modality contribution
and examine whether the adapted model recovers the expected cortical topography.
sections.content: Design. For each window, we compute exact Shapley values over the three input modalities, {video, audio, text}. modality is ablated by replacing its input embeddings with content-free mean embedding while preserving token count, position, and temporal alignment (Lundberg and Lee, 2017). Therefore, only stimulus information is removed. Evaluating all eight (23) modality subsets yields an exact additive decomposition of each modalitys contribution to encoding performance. The same decomposition can also tell us through which token positions each modalitys information reaches the readout. At every timestep, the readout takes three hidden states, one for each modality, at the truncated layer. After many layers of attention, however, each of these states can carry information from all three input modalities, so audio information, for example, may reach the readout through video token. sections.title:
5.5 Training a population of independently adapted models
Efficient multi-adapter training. To efficiently train many adapters, we develop a specialized multi-LoRA
training kernel. Since LoRA modules are small and structurally identical, the routed updates for N adapters
can be fused into a single batched gather–matrix multiplication, enabling parallel training of N adapters
together (Fig. 5a). The speedup arises from improved hardware utilization rather than reduced FLOPs: at
N =32, the fused step costs only 1.08x a single-adapter step, yielding a 29.8x speedup over sequential training.
End-to-end speedups are smaller because of longer sequences and larger batches. See App. C for details.
sections.content: Large-scale ensemble performance. We train 261 independently adapted models spanning different hyperparameters, readout architectures, and backbones, and aggregate with parcel-wise minimum-variance ensemble combiner fitted on out-of-fold predictions (App. G). Ensemble accuracy reaches 0.3483 on validation, 0.3428 on ID, and 0.2483 on OOD, achieving the top score on the public post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing, outperforming unpublished submissions as well (Tab. 1). All reported models were selected using validation performance only. carefully selected 15-model subset reaches 0.3465 on validation, within 0.0018 of the full ensemble, at one seventeenth of the inference cost. Both the subset and its weights are chosen on the validation set (App. D). To characterize the effect of ensemble size, we score random subsets of the 261-model pool at every size and fit their mean accuracy with m(n) = Anb, which results in 0.94 (R2=0.998; Fig. 5b). An exponent near 1 is consistent with ensemble theory: if members residuals have mean pairwise correlation ρ, the ensembles residual variance is σ2[ρ + (1 ρ)/n] (Ueda and Nakano, 1996; Wood et al., 2023), whose second term shrinks as 1/n. The first term does not shrink with size, which sets the ceiling performance m. The ensemble ceiling thus depends on how correlated the members errors are (σ2ρ), and hence on the ensembles composition rather than its size alone. We next examine, at fixed pool size, what ensemble properties influence the performance. For random 20-model subsets, mean residual correlation and mean single-model performance explain 5% and 23% of the variance in ensemble score individually, but explain 97% of the variance jointly (Fig. 5c; Krogh and Vedelsby, 1994; Kuncheva and Whitaker, 2003; Douven et al., 2026). These factors are highly correlated in our pool (r=0.74), as models with more diversity tend to be weaker individually. Therefore, separate coefficients of the fit should not be read as the effect of changing one property while holding the other fixed. 9 Useful diversity arises primarily from changes in model architecture rather than minor training variations. Models with different readout architectures or backbones show substantially lower residual correlation with the rest of the pool. In contrast, changes in seed, LoRA rank, layer choice, or training data subset provide little diversity (Fig. 9, App. J).

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: Three axes for scaling PEFT for brain encoding. Together, our results suggest three complementary scaling directions for future brain encoding models: 1) Scale up the pretrained prior by leveraging increasingly capable backbones; 2) Scale down the adaptation by updating only small number of parameters; and 3) Scale out by training large number of lightweight adapters to shared backbones with various inductive biases (Mind Lab et al., 2026). Together, PEFT turns single powerful pretrained model into family of specialized encoding models without training each backbone from scratch. Toward brain foundation model. Our experiments do not constitute brain foundation model, but scaling along the three directions discussed above could lead to one. large pretrained backbone could use single shared adapter trained on neural data spanning tasks, datasets, subjects, and even species. In this work, we only scale out the number of adapters for ensemble. However, future work could train separate adapter for each task, dataset, subject, or even ROI with hierarchical structure or with meta-learning. Together, this hierarchical approach and the three scaling directions we discuss above can create brain foundation model with efficient specializations for different downstream tasks. Limitations. Our models are trained on one benchmark with four subjects, all watching audiovisual narrative. The adapters transfer to held-out subject (App. M) and to second dataset (App. N), but neither test leaves the domain of narrative film. We leave the joint training on multiple datasets and modalities to future work.

sections.title: A Extended related work
sections.content: The full version of 2, by family: where does the neural signal enter the encoding model pipeline? Frozen backbone, trained readout. The dominant paradigm freezes model pretrained on behavioral or self-supervised task and fits readout from its hidden states to neural responses: the lineage running from voxelwise ridge regression (Naselaris et al., 2011; Huth et al., 2016; Nunez-Elizalde et al., 2019) through taskoptimized network comparisons (Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016; Schrimpf et al., 2021; Caucheteux and King, 2022) to todays multimodal encoders. Every leading entry in the Algonauts 2025 challenge leaderboard (Gifford et al., 2025) followed this paradigm, including MIRAGE (Gokce et al., 2026a), which we build on directly, TRIBE (dAscoli et al., 2026) and VIBE (Carlström Schad et al., 2025). retrospective report argued that architectural choices mattered less than ensembling (Scotti and Tripathy, 2025). Readout design has been studied on its own terms (Adeli et al., 2025; Lurz et al., 2021), and larger readout does not necessarily lead to higher accuracy: an ROI-query transformer readout is 37M against classical ridges 1,200M, yet it performs better (Adeli et al., 2025). Concurrent work (Zhang et al., 2026) reports strong OOD score on the Algonauts 2025 leaderboard using pool of frozen-backbone models with linear readouts, whose per-participant, per-film parameters were selected using public leaderboard scores. By contrast, we selected all models and ensemble weights on validation data alone (App. D). Backbones fine-tuned by brain data. second family updates the stimulus models own weights from neural recordings. Inducing brain-relevant bias in language models (Schwartz et al., 2019; Toneva and Wehbe, 2019) leads to brain-tuning of speech models, which improves not only alignment but also downstream semantic tasks (Moussa et al., 2025; Moussa and Toneva, 2025). The vision analogue trains with neural regularization and gains robustness and behavioral alignment (Li et al., 2019; Federer et al., 2020; Safarani et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2026). Our methods fall under this family, and parameter-efficient adaptation is already used within it: BrainWavLM brain-tunes with LoRA and matches full fine-tune (Vattikonda et al., 2025), and rank-8 LoRA at 0.625% of parameters suffices for cross-participant brain-tuning (Moussa and Toneva, 2025); MEM won the Algonauts 2023 challenge by adapting vision backbone with LoRA (Yang et al., 2023); recent work RABBiT achieves SoTA on audio cortex prediction by adapting an audio backbone (Moussa and Toneva, 2026). Although several works have explored PEFT for brain encoding, this remains relatively underexplored paradigm in the literature. What is new about our work is mainly the scale: the largest backbones whose weights have been updated by brain data are around 10B (Scholz et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026), and models above 15B appear in this literature only as frozen feature extractors. Concurrent work (Zhang et al., 2026) also trains LoRA experts inside omni-modal models of up to 104B total parameters, but supervises them with labels derived from fMRI networks rather than with the brain-encoding objective of predicting neural responses. We adapt backbones up to 104B for brain encoding, and we test them on whole-brain encoding benchmark rather than on specific brain area or for downstream task transfer. Joint task and brain-alignment objectives. third family trains primary objective together with an auxiliary alignment term against neural data (Dapello et al., 2023; Pirlot et al., 2022). The binding constraint is that the stimuli with recordings are tiny fraction of the task corpus, which is precisely the asymmetry parameter-efficient adaptation is built for. This family also involves some methodological warning signs: shuffledor permuted-target controls sometimes reproduce much of the reported benefit (Federer et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2025), so gain from neural supervision has to be shown against matched compute. We hold ourselves to the same standard throughout (5.3), and run the shifted-target control (App. L). Brain-only pretraining, aligned afterwards. fourth family pretrains self-supervised on neural data alone across subjects, sessions and datasets: masked autoencoding for fMRI (Ortega Caro et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2024; Lane et al., 2026), EEG (Jiang et al., 2024, 2025), intracranial recordings (Wang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024) and other modalities, and attaches the stimulus afterwards. It is worth noting that the most recent of these methods adapts large pretrained backbone with LoRA rather than training from scratch (Wu et al., 2026), the same direction we are going. No model in this family has been shown to beat specialized encoder on voxelwise correlation; they aim for decoding or semantic-level proxies instead. Batched multi-adapter kernels. Routing one batch of tokens to many adapters is solved problem for inference: Punicas segmented gather matmul (Chen et al., 2024) and S-LoRAs paged adapter pool (Sheng et al., 2024) both handle it. Because serving needs no gradients, neither system provides backward pass. Training systems are more recent and batch per adapter, with each adapter receiving its own inputs, so every group is full sequence (Yan et al., 2026; Zuo et al., 2026). The per-token form of the primitive instead comes from mixture-of-experts training, where MegaBlocks pads groups to block multiples (Gale et al., 2023) and ScatterMoE does not (Tan et al., 2024); stock PyTorch now also ships differentiable grouped matmul that takes distinct matrix per group. Neither the operator nor our two design choices (gathering rather than padding, and carrying the adapter index on grid dimension) is new. What is specific to our method is the regime. Grouped matmuls are designed for many tokens per group, whereas pool with one adapter per model, subject or parcel sits at the opposite extreme, where each group holds only handful of rows. In that regime, the fused kernels cost is nearly independent of pool size, while the alternatives costs grow with it. At the pool sizes used in this paper, this is merely speedup; if we were to train one adapter per parcel, our kernel would make training feasible at all (6).

sections.title: H Alternative PEFT methods
sections.content: All other adaptation results in this paper use LoRA. To test whether the gain depends on the method, we ran two further PEFT families under the same protocol: same backbone, feature extraction layer, context lead, readout, readout learning rate, step budget and seed. Only the adaptation method changes, and all configurations are compared with the same frozen control. IA3 (Liu et al., 2022) learns three element-wise rescaling vectors per decoder block, on the keys, Methods. the values and the FFN intermediate activations, and adds no weights. We run the standard attention + FFN scope and variant that also rescales the intermediate activations of the MoE experts, which LoRA does not touch. Bottleneck adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019) insert (cid:55) x+Wup gelu(Wdownx) into the residual stream. Unlike LoRA, this update is nonlinear and cannot be merged into the frozen weights. sections.title: J Why seeds are not a source of diversity
sections.content: 5.5 reports that changing the seed gives almost no ensemble gain, whereas changing the readout or the backbone does. Using the 15 seeds of the main configuration, we show that adapters trained from different seeds compute nearly the same function, so their predictions have little independent content to average. Weights. Updates from two seeds are nearly orthogonal in weight space: cos(Wi, Wj) = 0.026, at relative distance of 1.396 2. This follows from the parameterization. = BA lies in the row space of A, which is drawn at random and changes little during training, so any two seeds are orthogonal regardless of what they compute. The update is not small: its largest singular value is 0.60.8 of the frozen matrixs. Adapters should therefore be compared on activations rather than weights. 26 Activations. Fig. 9 compares each seeds change relative to the frozen backbone at increasing depth. On real inputs, single modules output change agrees at 0.151. The composed feature change agrees at 0.355 after one layer, 0.595 after sixteen, and 0.860 at the feature extraction layer, where it is still 45% of the feature norm. Agreement falls back to 0.740.82 by the final layer (Fig. 9b). The rise is not explained by independent per-layer noise averaging out: model of independent per-layer noise, fitted at layer 1, predicts 0.820.87 by layer 8, against an observed 0.430.54. Readout and prediction. Pairing an adapter with another seeds jointly trained readout costs 0.0012, and with another seeds re-fit readout 0.0024, both inside the seed spread. Under one shared readout, the prediction change is 0.418 of the prediction norm and = 0.934 correlated across seeds, with shared fraction 1 0.939 = 0.104 of prediction. of 0.939. Each seeds deviation from the consensus is therefore 0.418 The ensemble analysis measures this member-specific component independently, from the members own predictions, and finds that it correlates with the fMRI target at 0.003. The seed-specific part of prediction is thus small and carries no signal, and it is what averaging over seeds removes. This is why seed-only pools saturate by 12 members while member with different readout or backbone still adds accuracy (App. G).

Nine low-level stimulus statistics (luminance, contrast, motion energy and cuts from the frames; RMS, envelope modulation and spectral centroid from the audio; words per TR and speech on/off from the transcript), lagged 09 s, explain the shared residual at only = 0.027 under episodelevel cross-validation.
